title: Protein Function Predictor
blurb: Exploring AI-based protein function prediction from amino-acid sequences.
lede: Developing a protein function prediction project and a focused research study on how protein language-model representations generalize to less familiar sequences.

paras: A protein function prediction system that takes amino-acid sequences as input and predicts Gene Ontology labels describing protein activity, biological roles, and cellular location. The project is in development.
My work with ProTeam includes the project overview, system architecture, presentations, and dashboard planning.
Can a model using ESM-2 protein sequence embeddings improve function prediction compared with a DeepGOPlus-style baseline, especially for proteins with low similarity to the training data?

Compare a lightweight multi-label classifier on frozen ESM-2 embeddings with a DeepGOPlus-style baseline using consistent labels, data partitions, and evaluation rules. Start with molecular function and use CAFA3 alongside a fixed UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot release.

The planned evaluation reports Fmax and area under the precision-recall curve, both overall and for a predefined low-similarity subset. The expected output is a reproducible comparison, performance charts, and an analysis of model limitations. Improvements remain hypotheses to test; experimental results are not yet claimed.

title: WaterSight
blurb: AI water intelligence for Texas, meant to reach communities before they hit crisis rather than after. It started with one storm and two very different neighborhoods.
lede: AI-powered water intelligence that bridges the gap before communities reach crisis. A single-file app running the Claude API over county-level Texas map data, combining climate modeling with AI reasoning into plain guidance for planners, farmers, and policymakers.

stats.label: people facing a water crisis daily, worldwide
needed by 2040 for US water infrastructure

paras: I saw the problem driving Uber in downtown Houston. Heavy rain, water rising, sewers struggling. Ten minutes later, in a different neighborhood: waist-deep flooding, families walking through it, lost pets, infrastructure that clearly was not built for this. Same storm, same city, completely different outcome depending on the neighborhood. That gap is the whole reason WaterSight exists.

Money is already pointed at this problem — $55B from the federal Infrastructure Law, $35T in ESG and impact funds, $30B+ from the World Bank across 100+ countries since 2010, $10B+ from corporates like Coca-Cola, Nestlé, and Microsoft. The problem isn't money. It's connectivity. That single line is the core of the pitch, and it is the same thesis behind Terrasite.

rows.v: 150,000 people without safe water for weeks
100,000 people drank poisoned water for years
80,000 homes built with no guaranteed water
21 million people depend on aquifers that are running dry

paras: Investors pay $25,000 a year for company water profiles, ESG scores, and investment signals. Companies pay from $10,000 a project for a featured, verified profile. Residents get water quality alerts, conservation tips, and infrastructure updates free, forever — that is the point, not a growth tactic. Equity means a free tier for underserved communities, privacy means encryption and no personal information collected, bias means auditing for geographic skew, and transparency means publishing the methodology and the inputs.

Fifteen slides at the PVAMU AI Innovation Challenge 2026, structured wide to narrow and back out: global scale, one personal story, the national crisis, the money already in play, the gap, the product, the business. The emotional anchor is Mrs. Smith in Jackson, Mississippi, turning on a faucet for her grandchildren and getting nothing, then boiling river water for weeks. The closing slide returns to her. Design was deliberately cinematic and minimal — clarity over complexity.
Growth path from there: $1–3M in year one on a Texas pilot plus other states, $5–15M by year three on municipal and API expansion, $15–20M by year five at national scale.

title: Vital Handoff
blurb: Turning the Apple Watch into a witness during an emergency: detect the crisis on-device, capture the last 30 minutes of vitals, hand it to a responder as a QR code on the lock screen.
lede: No one should be invisible in an emergency. In the Golden Hour, the first sixty minutes, medical professionals make life-or-death decisions in an information vacuum. Vital Handoff closes that gap with hardware people already own.

stats.label: of continuous vitals captured before handoff
a watch, against $40,000 for an ICU stay

paras: My teammate Kamron broke his arm in three places catching a football at twelve years old. The ER nurse called it a bruise — no inspection, no data, no time. A specialist found the three fractures later by MRI. Four hours where the system failed him, and he still has the metal implants.

rows.v: The watch monitors vitals through HealthKit; on-device AI recognizes a crisis in real time
The last 30 minutes of biometrics become a structured medical summary, then a single secure QR code
The code appears on the lock screen; one scan opens the full Golden Hour dashboard and emergency contacts are notified automatically

paras: Apple Watch Series 9 plus iPhone, so there is zero hardware cost for anyone already inside the ecosystem. Crisis detection is on-device via Apple Intelligence. Data stays in the Secure Enclave, encrypted, under the user's control until the moment it is needed, and only then transmits to EMS. The responder view puts ECG, heart rate, blood pressure, SpO2, and temperature on the left with status flags, and demographics, allergies, medications, past surgeries, and conditions on the right — complex health data turned into a clear, actionable story.

The business case aligns everyone in the room. Hospitals turn an expense into revenue by billing insurance for remote patient monitoring. Insurers compare $400 for a watch against $40,000 for an ICU stay. Once integrated, the handoff becomes the standard entry point for ER data. Launch is through localized clinical pilots with regional EMS teams and hospital networks, aimed first at people with severe allergies, chronic illness, and elderly patients prone to emergencies.
The five-year version predicts cardiac events before the patient loses consciousness and routes them to the nearest EMS automatically — the right care to the right person at the right time.

title: On Record
blurb: A civic transparency app showing where local officials stand on data center development, who funds them, and when you can speak.
lede: Local officials decide where data centers get built, those votes are close, and almost nobody watching knows how their representative voted or who paid for their campaign. On Record puts money, votes, and stated position on one screen, each linked to the public database it came from.

stats.label: the Prince William vote that approved the largest data center project in the world
slide deck that runs inside the app itself

paras: In December 2023 Prince William County, Virginia approved what was then the largest data center project in the world. The vote was four to three. Most residents found out afterward. That is how these decisions get made — not in Congress, but by a county board on a Tuesday night in a room with forty people in it, on margins that are coin flips: Virginia Senate 21 to 17, Virginia House 63 to 34.

In July 2026 the same Prince William board denied a 2,000 acre proposal eight to nothing, after a five hour hearing, because the room was full and the analysis was done. The information changed the vote. That gap, between a decision being public and a decision being known, is the entire product.

rows.v: No account, no address, no signup wall
Sorted by where they stand on data center development
Who funds them, how they voted, and what they said — three things that normally live in three separate government systems, each linked to its source database
The date of the next meeting where public comment is on the agenda
A community feed of votes, filings, and news; an events page with agenda and RSVP; a facilities map plotting proposed and operating data centers with capacity and daily water draw

sections.h: Design decisions I would defend in a room
paras: Non-partisan by construction, not by disclaimer. Every color that could imply a position is good or bad was removed — Supports, Mixed, and Opposes render in the same green, distinguished by shape: filled, half, and hollow circle. Votes and donors carry no valence color either. The side effect is that stance stays readable for colorblind users without a separate accessibility pass.

Funding sits next to position, with no causal claim. The product shows the share of an official's disclosed funding coming from data center, technology, and energy donors, directly beside their stance, and never says the money bought the vote. In the real Prince William case the supervisor who received the most industry money voted against the project. That is precisely why both numbers are on screen and the conclusion is left to the reader — the moment the product editorializes, it is just another advocacy site.

No accounts, on purpose. Guest mode is the default path. Data centers get sited near lower income neighborhoods, so a tool that only works for people with time, broadband, and a willingness to hand over an email address makes the problem it addresses worse. The sign-in animation deliberately shows no credential fields: it reads as connecting to public records, not as a gate.

Fictional names, real sources. Every official, stance, vote, and contribution in the app is illustrative sample data with a deliberately fictional name, while offices, districts, and source systems are real. Publishing invented voting records attached to real people would have destroyed the credibility the whole product rests on.

rows.v: One file knows where data comes from and every component consumes its return types, so moving from seed data to Postgres means rewriting function bodies rather than touching components. The matching schema is already written, mirroring the TypeScript types field for field.

A covered city resolves from almost any input — Houston, houston, Houston TX, htown, htx, 77002, Harris County, Katy, Cypress, or a partial like hous. Unrecognized input shows one-tap chips for every covered area, never an error. No input leaves a user stuck and none can break a live demo.

A Houston town hall is at 6:30 PM in Houston regardless of where the laptop is. Every event carries an IANA zone passed explicitly to Intl — without it the runtime silently shifts the time to the viewer's zone, which for a civic calendar sends people to a meeting at the wrong hour.
Every presentation figure is computed from the app's own data, so the deck can never drift from the live product. External statistics live in a separate file and cannot be added without a citation.

rows.k: The deck is part of the app
rows.v: A seven-slide presentation runs at /presentation with keyboard and clicker nav, URL-persisted position so a refresh keeps your place, clickable progress dots for Q&A, and a handoff button that opens the product.

paras: Every claim links to the database that holds that kind of record: Texas Ethics Commission for contributions, Houston City Secretary for ordinances, Texas Legislature Online for bills, Harris County Commissioners Court for orders, ERCOT for grid filings. Because the prototype's individual records are illustrative, links resolve to each system's search page rather than a fabricated deep link that would 404. In production the search URL is swapped for a specific filing ID and the display layer does not change.

This is a prototype. It runs entirely on local seed data with no database and no API keys, which is what made it demoable anywhere with no network dependency except the map tiles. Genuinely built: the full navigation flow, the data seam, the schema, the sourcing layer, the accessibility model, and the deck. Not built: ingestion, accounts, and an editorial backend.

Next: community groups with discussion threads, template letters pre-filled with the user's district, an admin backend for editing stances with attached evidence, automated ingestion from TEC, FEC, and legislative record systems, and real accounts with a saved location.

paras: Data centers are the fastest growing land use fight in the country and the one decided at a level almost nobody watches. The structure is not specific to them — warehouses, pipelines, landfills, transmission lines: same decision-making body, same information gap, same fix.

title: On Record: Research
blurb: The evidence base behind On Record — every figure a published number with a citation that resolves.
lede: Data center siting is decided by county boards, city councils, and state legislatures. Is that a real information gap, and is the gap consequential — do the decisions turn on margins small enough that an informed public could change them? Both answers are yes, and the second one is what justified building anything.

sections.h: The scale is national and accelerating
paras: Load roughly tripled in a decade and is on track to triple again in five years. The power and the water come from somewhere, and the somewhere is decided locally.

sections.h: The decisive votes are close, and local
paras: This is the finding that produced the product. These are not landslides. The PW Digital Gateway rezoning passed four to three after a marathon hearing, and the project later collapsed when developers dropped their appeal in April 2026. The large-user cost allocation measure — which would let the State Corporation Commission assign costs driven by large users to those users rather than to households — passed 21 to 17 in the Senate and 63 to 34 in the House.

The contrast is the argument. The same board that approved a project four to three in 2023 denied a larger one eight to nothing in 2026, after a five hour hearing with a full room and completed analysis. Information moved a unanimous vote.

rows.v: PW Digital Gateway rezoning, Dec 2023 — 4 to 3 (Data Center Dynamics)
Large-user electricity cost allocation — 21 to 17 (NCEL)
House companion to the ratepayer measure — 63 to 34
Dulles Cloud South, ~2,000 acres and 43M sq ft, denied 8 to 0 on 7 Jul 2026 after a five hour hearing (Potomac Local News)

sections.h: States are already writing the rules
paras: The regulatory vocabulary already exists. What residents lack is not policy language, it is knowing which meeting to attend and what their official has already done.

rows.v: Signed 21 Jun 2025 — facilities over 75 MW face mandatory curtailment during grid emergencies and must support remote disconnection (Baker Botts)
Directs the utility to seek rates making large users of 25 MW and above pay for the generating capacity they require
Permit process for facilities over 100 MW, including sound assessments where homes or schools sit within 500 feet
Water utilities must report monthly volumes supplied to data centers; applicants must file annual water consumption estimates before rezoning

paras: Research that only confirmed the hypothesis would have produced a worse product. Money does not predict the vote: in the Prince William case the supervisor who received the most data center industry money voted against the project. That single fact set the product's central editorial constraint — show funding and position side by side, make no causal claim, let the reader draw the conclusion. A tool that implied donation therefore vote would have been falsified by its own founding case study.

Not every facility is equivalent either. A well-sited facility with closed-loop cooling uses a fraction of the water of a conventional build, and residents can only reward that difference if someone puts the numbers side by side. The product is built to let a good facility win on the record, not to oppose data centers.

Beyond the statistics, the research catalogued which public database actually holds each kind of record, since the product's promise is that every claim is checkable. Every URL was verified to resolve; three return 403 to automated checks but load normally in a browser.

What the audit revealed: the records are public and already published on a schedule, but scattered across separate systems with separate search interfaces. One gives you money, another gives you votes, a county agenda system gives you the meeting. No single system puts money, votes, and stated position on one screen for one local official on one specific issue, and none organizes any of it around when a resident can next speak. It is an aggregation and timing problem, not a disclosure problem.

rows.v: Texas Ethics Commission, FEC, OpenSecrets, FollowTheMoney, Virginia Department of Elections, Arizona See The Money, Ohio Secretary of State
Texas Legislature Online, Houston City Secretary, Harris County Commissioners Court, Virginia LIS, Loudoun County, Maricopa County, Ohio Legislature
ERCOT, US Energy Information Administration, EPA Envirofacts, Texas Water Development Board, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory

paras: Data center siting concentrates near lower income neighborhoods. That is what made access constraints a design requirement rather than a nice-to-have: a tool that only works for people with time, broadband, and an email address to spend would widen the very gap it exists to close. Adopted at build time rather than as later cleanup: no account required ever, runs on an older phone, free, position shown as a shape and a word rather than color alone, and English first followed by the top two other languages spoken in each launch city.

sections.h: How the research is held in the code
paras: The verified findings live in their own file, isolated from the illustrative demo data by an explicit rule written into the file header: nothing enters the research file without a citation a reader can open and check. Source systems live in a second file, and presentation figures derived from demo data in a third, computed from the seed itself so the pitch and the product cannot disagree. Keeping that boundary bright in the file structure, rather than in a convention, is what let the deck cite real numbers and the app show sample officials without either one contaminating the other.
